rationale: The abstract examines specific legal and fiscal infrastructure-financing rules—nineteenth-century property special assessments in Chicago and 1987 development impact fees in Phoenix—and how they shift infrastructure costs across space and social groups. However, the title and abstract refer generically to 'urban infrastructure' and 'public works' without specifying whether domestic water or sanitation/sewerage systems and household service access or affordability outcomes are empirically analysed. Under sensitivity-preserving Title/Abstract rules, full-text review is required to verify Criteria 1, 3 and 4.
plain_vs_narrow_note: No difference between narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings: municipal special assessments and development impact fees are explicit legal/regulatory cost-allocation mechanisms under both readings, while uncertainty stems from whether water/sanitation service access and empirical access outcomes are specifically analysed within 'urban infrastructure'.

evidence_quotes.quote: This article compares the financing of urban infrastructure in nineteenth-century Chicago and twentieth-century Phoenix, highlighting distributional conflicts over the cost of public goods.

I examine the history of adoption and implementation of development impact fees, which were intended to "make growth pay for itself" by assessing new development to finance infrastructure it would require
efforts to shift the cost of public goods over space, time, and social groups or classes in growing communities.
